response: Read the finding and the file itself. Here's the diagnosis and the plan. ## The finding `crime_00034` — **SVG With Embedded Raster**, severity `high`, confidence `0.95`, on `src/assets/partner-logo.svg`. Quoting the evidence verbatim: > - `2 `` occurrences` > - `embedded MIME types: image/jpeg, image/png` > - `SVG byte size: 592 bytes (includes the base64 overhead)` > - `re-author the raster region as vector paths, or split it out to its own asset` So: **2 embedded rasters**, MIME types **`image/jpeg`** and **`image/png`**. ## What's actually in the file `src/assets/partner-logo.svg` is 5 lines. A `200×80` viewBox containing a `` and two `<image>` elements — and nothing else. There is not one vector primitive in it: no `<path>`, `<rect>`, `<circle>`, or `<text>`. The file is a wrapper around two data URIs: - `partner-logo.svg:3` — `<image x="0" y="0" width="80" height="80" href="data:image/png;base64,…">` - `partner-logo.svg:4` — `<image x="100" y="0" width="80" height="80" xlink:href="data:image/jpeg;base64,…">` Two things worth noting beyond the finding: 1. **Line 4 uses `xlink:href` but the root `<svg>` declares no `xmlns:xlink`.** That's a malformed document — strict parsers and some sanitizers will drop the attribute and render nothing where the second mark should be. Whatever you do about the rasters, that attribute has to change to plain `href` (SVG 2) or the namespace has to be declared. 2. The 592-byte size is not reassuring. Both payloads here are 1×1 pixel stubs blown up to `80×80` — the byte count is small *because the pixels are placeholder-sized*, not because embedding is cheap. Swap in the real marks and base64 inflates them ~33% over the binary, inside a file that no CDN can serve as an image and no browser can cache separately from the SVG. `grep` for `partner-logo` across the repo's `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.md`/`.json`/`.css` returns nothing, so there is no import site to update — the asset is referenced only by whatever ships it. That makes the refactor low-risk, but it also means you can't infer the intended render size from a call site; keep the `200×80` viewBox as the contract. ## Remediation **Split by what each region actually is.** The two images are different MIME types for a reason, and that reason decides their fate: **Left mark (`image/png`, x=0) → re-author as vector paths.** PNG here signals flat color with hard edges and transparency — a logo mark or wordmark. That is exactly what SVG geometry is for. Open the partner's original vector source (Illustrator/Figma/brand kit) and export the mark as paths. If no vector source exists, ask the partner for one; a logo without vector source is a brand-asset problem, not a code problem. Only if the partner genuinely cannot supply one should you fall back to auto-tracing — and auto-traced paths need a visual diff against the raster before they ship, because tracers mangle small counters and tight corners. **Right mark (`image/jpeg`, x=100) → split out to a standalone raster.** JPEG is a lossy continuous-tone codec; nobody encodes a flat logo as JPEG. This is a photograph or a gradient-heavy badge, and vectorising it is the wrong move — a trace would produce hundreds of paths, render slower than the bitmap, and look worse. Externalise it: decode the base64 to a real file, re-encode as WebP (with a PNG fallback if you support anything that predates WebP), and reference it by URL. **Concrete steps:** 1. Decode both data URIs to disk to see what you're dealing with — `base64 -d` on each payload. Confirm the PNG is flat-color and the JPEG is continuous-tone before committing to the split above; if the JPEG turns out to be flat art badly exported, it goes down the vector path too. 2. Obtain vector source for the left mark and export as paths into the SVG, preserving the `0 0 200 80` viewBox and the mark's `80×80` box at `x=0`. 3. Write the right-hand image out as `src/assets/partner-badge.webp`, sized to the dimensions it renders at (`80×80` CSS px, so `160×160` for 2× DPI — don't ship more pixels than that). 4. Replace line 4's `<image>` with `<image x="100" y="0" width="80" height="80" href="./partner-badge.webp"/>`, using plain `href`, and delete the `xlink:` usage entirely. 5. Drop the now-unneeded raster: the left `<image>` element disappears, replaced by the path geometry. 6. Re-run `crimes scan --format json` and confirm `svg_with_embedded_raster` no longer fires on this file. **One caveat on step 4:** an SVG that references an external image by relative URL will render that image when loaded as a document or via `<img src>`, but **not** when inlined into HTML in some contexts, and never when the SVG is embedded as a CSS `background-image` data URI. If the consuming code inlines this SVG, the external reference silently renders blank. In that case the right shape is not one SVG at all — it's `partner-logo.svg` (pure vector, left mark only) plus `partner-badge.webp` as a sibling asset, composed by the markup that renders them side by side rather than by the SVG. ## Files after the refactor - **`src/assets/partner-logo.svg`** — kept, still shipping. Pure vector: `<title>`, `<path>` geometry for the left mark, and either an external `href` to the badge or nothing at all if you go with the two-asset composition. - **`src/assets/partner-badge.webp`** — new. The continuous-tone right-hand image, sized to render dimensions. - Optionally **`src/assets/partner-badge.png`** — fallback, only if your browser support matrix needs it. The file is not deleted at any point; the logo keeps shipping throughout, and the viewBox and rendered dimensions stay identical so nothing downstream reflows.
